match-components.title: Robot parts and their jobs
match-components.instructions: Tap a robot part on the left, then tap the job it does on the right. You can also drag a part onto its job.

pairs.right: Detects information about the surroundings
pairs.why: Sensors are the robot's senses: light, distance, temperature, touch.

pairs.right: Processes inputs and decides what to do
pairs.why: The controller (for example an Arduino) is the robot's brain.

pairs.right: Produces movement
pairs.why: Motors, servos and cylinders turn energy into motion.

pairs.right: Provides energy to all the parts
pairs.why: Batteries or mains supply power the controller, sensors and actuators.

pairs.right: Tool at the end of the arm that does the task
pairs.why: Grippers, welding torches and suction cups are end effectors.

match-electronics.title: Components and their functions
match-electronics.instructions: Match each electronic component to its function.

pairs.right: Limits electric current
pairs.why: A resistor opposes current, for example to protect an LED.

pairs.right: Stores electric charge
pairs.why: Capacitors store and release charge, smoothing supplies.

pairs.right: Switches or amplifies small signals
pairs.why: A small base current controls a larger collector current.

pairs.right: Heavy-duty switch for high-power loads
pairs.why: A contactor is a big relay used for motors and other high-power devices.

pairs.right: Protects a circuit from too much current
pairs.why: It trips and cuts the supply in an overload or short circuit.

pairs.right: Gives an adjustable voltage
pairs.why: Turning the knob moves the wiper along the track, changing the output voltage.

pairs.right: Lets current flow one way only
pairs.why: Used to protect circuits from reverse current, for example across motors.

match-actuators.title: Actuators and their energy sources
match-actuators.instructions: Match each actuator to the energy source that drives it.

pairs.right: Electric current from a battery
pairs.why: Electric actuators turn electrical energy into rotation.

pairs.right: Pressurised liquid (oil)
pairs.why: Hydraulics use a liquid. They give very large forces, as in excavators.

pairs.right: Compressed air
pairs.why: Pneumatics use a gas. They are fast and clean, good for pick-and-place.

pairs.right: Magnetic field from a current-carrying coil
pairs.why: The coil pulls an iron plunger in, giving a short straight push or pull.

pairs.right: Heat
pairs.why: The wire contracts when heated by a current and relaxes when it cools.

match-mechanisms.title: Mechanisms and motion
match-mechanisms.instructions: Match each mechanism to what it does to motion.

pairs.right: Turns rotary motion into straight (linear) motion
pairs.why: The pinion gear drives the toothed rack backwards and forwards.

pairs.right: Turns rotation into a rising and falling motion
pairs.why: The cam profile pushes the follower up and a spring returns it.

pairs.right: Changes speed and torque
pairs.why: A small gear driving a big gear gives more torque and less speed.

pairs.right: Allows rotation in one direction only
pairs.why: The pawl catches on the teeth to stop the wheel turning back.

pairs.right: Turns rotation into back-and-forth motion
pairs.why: Like a bicycle pedal or engine piston, used in walking robots.

match-locomotion.title: Locomotion and terrain
match-locomotion.instructions: Match each way of moving to the terrain it suits best.

pairs.right: Smooth, flat floors such as a factory or classroom
pairs.why: Wheels are fast and energy efficient on smooth surfaces.

pairs.right: Mud, sand and loose soil
pairs.why: Tracks spread the weight over a large area so they do not sink, and they grip well.

pairs.right: Rocky ground with gaps and steps
pairs.why: Legs can step over obstacles and keep traction on uneven ground.

pairs.right: Through the air over roads and rivers
pairs.why: Drones fly over obstacles, as in medical deliveries to rural areas.

pairs.right: Underwater
pairs.why: Underwater robots push against water to move and steer.

flowchart-symbols.title: Flowchart symbol quiz
flowchart-symbols.instructions: Match each flowchart symbol to what it means.

pairs.right: Start or stop
pairs.why: Every flowchart begins and ends with an oval (terminator).

pairs.right: Process (an action such as Move forward)
pairs.why: Rectangles show something the robot does.

pairs.right: Input or output (such as Read sensor)
pairs.why: Reading a sensor or displaying a value is input or output.

pairs.right: Decision with Yes and No branches
pairs.why: A question such as Obstacle detected? has two exits.

pairs.right: Flow line showing the order of steps
pairs.why: Arrows connect the symbols and show the direction of flow.

loop-sorter.title: Open loop or closed loop?
loop-sorter.instructions: Drag each example into the right bin, or tap an example and then tap a bin.

items.why: It toasts for a set time and never checks how brown the bread is.
The thermostat measures room temperature and switches cooling on or off.
IR sensors detect the line and the robot corrects its steering.
It moves by a fixed amount and cannot check where it ended up.

items.text: Washing machine on a fixed cycle
items.why: It runs for set times and does not measure how clean the clothes are.

items.text: Wall-following robot with an ultrasonic sensor
items.why: It measures the distance to the wall and corrects it.

items.text: Traffic lights on a fixed timer
items.why: They change on time, not according to the traffic.
The thermostat cuts the heater when the set temperature is reached.

sort-printing.title: FDM or SLA?
sort-printing.instructions: Sort each property into the 3D printing method it describes.

items.text: Melts plastic filament through a hot nozzle
items.why: FDM means Fused Deposition Modelling: it lays down melted plastic.

items.text: Cures liquid resin with UV light
items.why: SLA (stereolithography) hardens photopolymer resin with a laser or UV screen.
These are thermoplastic filaments for FDM printers.
SLA material is a light-sensitive liquid resin.

items.text: Very fine detail and smooth surface
items.why: SLA layers are very thin and the light spot is small.
PLA, PETG and ABS parts survive knocks, good for a robot chassis.
Cured resin can crack or snap under impact.

items.text: Cheaper, with a larger build volume
items.why: FDM printers and filament are cheaper and usually print bigger parts.

items.text: Parts need washing and UV post-curing
items.why: Uncured resin must be washed off and the part hardened fully.

items.text: Layer lines are easy to see
items.why: FDM layers are thicker, so lines show on the surface.

sort-revolutions.title: Industrial revolutions and technology
sort-revolutions.instructions: Sort each technology into the industrial revolution it belongs to.

items.why: Steam power drove the first factories and railways.
Machines replaced hand weaving in the first revolution.
Electric power was the key technology of the second revolution.
Moving assembly lines (for example Ford, 1913) made mass production possible.
Cheap steel made large machines and buildings possible.
Fast communication arrived in the second revolution.
Petrol and diesel engines powered cars and machines.
PLCs brought computer control to factory machines.
Unimate began work at General Motors in 1961, leading into the automation age.
Digital electronics and IT define the third revolution.
AI lets machines learn and make decisions.
Connected sensors and devices share data over the internet.
Physical machines tightly linked with software and data.

flowchart.title: Delivery vehicle flowchart (Paper 2 Q3(c))
flowchart.instructions: Place each block into the right slot by dragging it, or tap a block and then tap a slot. Then tap each yellow label to set it to Yes or No. Tap a placed block to send it back.
flowchart.explanation: Start, then Follow pre-defined path. Destination reached? Yes goes to Stop at destination. No goes on to Read obstacle sensor (a parallelogram because it is an input). At a junction? No loops back to Follow path. Yes asks Obstacle detected? No loops back to Follow path. Yes goes to Stop motors and wait, then back to Read obstacle sensor to check again.
